title: How the MONO Eraser Won Japan's #1 Color Trademark | Curio Archive
description:
That blue-white-black MONO eraser sitting in nearly every student's pencil case wasn't even sold on its own back in 1967—it started as a freebie tucked inside a dozen-pack of luxury MONO100 pencils. How did a giveaway overtake the flagship to claim roughly half of Japan's market, and pass a needle-eye gate of just 9 approvals out of ~560 filings to win Japan's very first pure-color trademark?
For anyone who has ever gripped a blue-white-black eraser and wondered about the business and IP strategy behind everyday stationery.

This episode starts in 1959, when Japan pioneered the PVC plastic eraser, then traces Tombow Pencil's 14-year lab effort from 1949 to pack 8 billion particles per cubic millimeter into the 1963 MONO and 1967 MONO100 pencils. One free plastic eraser per dozen worked so well that customer demand forced a 1969 standalone launch in a tricolor flag-inspired blue-white-black sleeve. We break down how the paper sleeve doubles as physical armor against PVC plasticizer sticking to desks and rulers, the design manual kept unchanged across five generations and four redesigns over half a century, Tombow's ~50% Japanese market share estimate in 2015, and why its 1999–2000 2D and 3D trademarks still left color-only copycats a loophole. Next, we follow Japan's April 1, 2015 opening of color-only trademarks under Article 3(2) of the Trademark Act: nationwide blind recognition surveys led to Registration No. 5930334 on March 10, 2017—Japan's first pure-color trademark (with Japan Patent Office (JPO) data showing only 9 approvals out of roughly 560 filings through June 2022). Just five months later, on August 18, 2017, Tombow stripped every letter off the sleeve for a wordless two-pack built for the National Center Test for University Admissions. Finally, we close with the 2019 50th-anniversary retro box, the 2011 Good Design Long Life Design Award, and the 2024 without whitening dye scallop-shell biomass edition that won another Good Design Award.

This channel has no affiliation with or sponsorship from any company or agency mentioned. All trademark registrations and historical figures come from public primary and institutional sources.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.

m053.text: The Japan Patent Office opened color-only marks.

m054.text: Approval let you own colors for your goods.

m055.text: Tombow filed on day one—how high was the bar?

m056.text: Japanese law assumes raw colors lack identity.

m057.text: Brands must prove decades of public recognition.

m063.text: Only nine won—well under two percent.
